10041032:
Catharine Gignac Holden LD 776
My name is Cathie Gignac. For the past 14 years I have worked in the greater Bangor area providing Behavioral Health services to children and their families. For the past 10 years I have worked as a case manager supporting children with behavioral and developmental challenges. I support these children and their families in identifying and accessing services to support in addressing these challenges. These services are provided to children through MaineCare.
During the pandemic, the federal government provided funding directed to provide free lunches to all school children. After this funding ended, the Maine State Legislature, with bipartisan support, passed LD 1679 which continued this funding in 2021. In August 2024, my fellow case managers and I were made aware that the Maine Department of Education had decided that this funding did not apply to Special Purpose Private Schools. Per the state of Maine website "special purpose private schools approved in Maine, as out-of-district placements to provide educational programming and crisis stabilization for students who are unable to access their education in a less restrictive setting". So, after a school has attempted to meet the behavioral and/or developmental challenges of a student and finds that they are not able to meet those needs, the student is referred to a special purpose private school. The student remains a registered student in the sending school department and the sending school pays a tuition for the student to attend. It is often not a choice but a necessity to send a student to these programs. There are 28 special purpose private schools in Maine.
At the start of school in 2024, at one particular school, parents were informed there would be a cost of $5.00 per day for lunch and an additional $2.50 if they were to have breakfast as well. This could total up to $150 a month for the family. Another school required students to provide their own meals. This school often had food, at the expense of the school, when students didn't have appropriate food to sustain them through the day. Another program I'm familiar with purchases food through the school district of the town they are located in.
As placement in special purpose private schools is often not a choice, I would like for you to consider extending the funding for free meals in schools to cover students at these schools as well.

Testimony of Colleen Foley-Ingersoll, M.Ed., BCBA, MaineHealth In Support of LD 776, "An Act to Provide Free School Lunches to Special Purpose Private Schools That Receive Students from the Public
School System" Monday, Mar 31, 2024
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonen, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, please accept this written testimony in support of LD 776, "An Act to Provide Free School Lunches to Special Purpose Private Schools That Receive Students from the Public School System."
MaineHealth is an integrated non-profit health care system that provides the full continuum of health care services to the residents of eleven counties in Maine and one in New Hampshire. As part of our vision of "Working Together So Maine's Communities are the Healthiest in America," MaineHealth, which includes MaineHealth Behavioral Health, is committed to creating a seamless system of behavioral healthcare across Maine, coordinating hospital psychiatric care with community-based treatment services, as well as residential treatment, and providing better access to behavioral healthcare through integration with primary care.
The Glickman Lauder Center of Excellence in Autism and Developmental Disorders (GLCOE), which serves individuals and their families through a continuum of care, including Early Intervention, Preschool, and K-12 programs. Our preschool and K-12 schools are private, Department of Education-approved institutions that serve children with autism and other developmental disorders.
GLCOE serves as a placement option for public school districts when a child's needs cannot be met within their local district. While GLCOE works closely with public schools, we are not part of the public school system. When a student requires an out-of-district placement, their Individual Education Plan (IEP) team may determine that GLCOE is the most suitable option for meeting the student's needs. This opportunity for a more tailored and specialized education can significantly enhance a child's learning, however, such a placement may result in the student losing access to certain opportunities provided by their local school district, including school meals.
Maine ranks 9th in the nation for food insecurity with 14.4% of Maine households being insecure. That equates to 1 in every 5 children. This highlights the significant burden that food insecurity places on families, particularly in the context of a specialized educational setting like GLCOE. To support these families, we advocate for expanding access to federally and statefunded child nutrition programs, to improve health equity across Maine.
Currently, GLCOE spends approximately $500 per month to provide food to our students, including breakfast, lunch, and snacks. This includes providing full meals to some students and

supplementing meals for others. We are currently working to partner with Westbrook School Department to offer meals that meet the National School Lunch Program standards. However, the cost per meal will be higher than the reimbursement rate, resulting in GLCOE incurring additional cost at approximately $0.40 per student per lunch and $0.25 per student per breakfast.
In closing, children in out of district placement deserve to have the same access to state-funded child nutrition programs. I urge you to support the legislation before you today.
Thank you,
Colleen Foley-Ingersoll Senior Director of the Developmental Disorders Services at Maine Behavioral Healthcare

10043910:
Maine Administrators of Services for Children with Disabilities

Testimony in Support of LD 776: An Act to Provide Free School Lunches to Special Purpose Private Schools That Receive Students from the Public School System

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Gay Anne McDonald and I am the Executive Director for the Maine Administrators of Services for Children with Disabilities (MADSEC).

Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony on behalf of the MADSEC Legislative Committee pursuant to LD 776: An Act to Provide Free School Lunches to Special Purpose Private Schools That Receive Students from the Public School System.

Currently, Maine provides free school meals to all public school students, a policy implemented to combat student hunger and promote better learning outcomes. However, we understand not all students receiving their education at special purpose private schools (SPPS) receive the same benefit. These schools, while serving publicly funded students, may not be eligible for, or are not receiving, the same meal reimbursement as public schools, leading to disparities for students with disabilities. SPPS are non-profit, state approved schools serving the most vulnerable public school students.

This discrepancy creates a practice where students, who would otherwise be enrolled in local public schools if not determined by the local IEP team, would receive meals at no cost to parents or the school. Such inequity undermines the foundational principle that all Maine students deserve the right to receive free, nutritious school meals to thrive educationally.

MADSEC is in no way an expert in school nutrition billing and it remains unclear whether reimbursement is already available to SPPS and hindered by procedural barriers, or whether legislative change is required to correct systemic oversight. However, whichever the case, MADSEC strongly believes that public school students who receive their education at SPPS should receive free meals - just as they would if attending their local public school.

If legislative change is required, MADSEC respectfully requests that the Committee move LD 776 forward as it aligns with Maine's commitment to ensure Maine public school students receive free meals and rectifies the current inequity. Respectfully, MADSEC would offer the recommendation to amend bill language to include public day treatment programs (regional programs).

Thank you for your time and upholding the state's responsibility to provide comprehensive support to every child under its care.
Gay Anne McDonald

Re: LD 776, An Act to Provide Free School Lunches to Special Purpose Private Schools That Receive Students from the Public School System

To: Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee

The Maine Chapter of the Freedom From Religion Foundation (MC-FFRF) writes in SUPPORT of LD 776.

Access to nutritious meals is a fundamental part of ensuring that students are able to learn in the classroom. School lunches have long been recognized as a vital component of a child's daily wellbeing, promoting not only physical health but also academic success. In Maine, the expansion of free school lunch programs to special purpose private schools is a much-needed step in creating a more equitable educational environment for all students.

Special purpose private schools provide the specialized support that their students need to succeed. However, students in these schools may face additional challenges when it comes to accessing adequate nutrition. Many families of children attending these schools may be from lower-income backgrounds. Children from low-income families are often disproportionately affected by food insecurity. This can lead to poor nutrition, which in turn impacts cognitive development, academic performance, and overall health. By providing free school lunches to students in special purpose private schools, Maine can help eliminate this barrier to success for many children who may not otherwise have access to nutritious food during the school day.

Children with special needs may face additional challenges when it comes to nutrition. Many students in these schools have unique medical or behavioral conditions that can make food insecurity and poor nutrition even more damaging. Children who have access to healthy meals are better able to concentrate and engage in the learning process. Nutritional meals also improve overall behavior and emotional well-being, which are crucial in a school environment, particularly in special purpose private schools where students may already face additional behavioral or emotional challenges.

Free school lunches in special purpose private schools would ensure that every student has the support needed to succeed in the classroom. No child should have to worry about when or where they will get their next meal, especially when that worry can interfere with their ability to learn and thrive. Special purpose private schools often serve children who may face challenges that are

not always addressed in traditional public school settings. For these students, access to free school lunches can be an important step in creating an environment where all students have the opportunity to succeed.
One of the major challenges faced by families and students who experience food insecurity is the stigma that often accompanies it. Children who do not have access to enough food may feel embarrassed or ashamed, which can further hinder their ability to succeed academically and socially. Providing free school lunches to students in special purpose private schools can help reduce this stigma, as all students would receive the same support and care. This can be especially important in special purpose private schools, where students may already be dealing with challenges related to their disabilities or needs. By ensuring that every student receives a meal, schools can create a more inclusive and supportive environment where all students are treated equally.
The positive impact on educational outcomes could have long-term benefits for the state as a whole. When children are well-nourished, they are more likely to stay engaged in school, graduate, and become productive members of society. Investing in free school lunches for special purpose private schools is an investment in Maine's future--one that benefits not only the children in these schools but also the broader community.
This is not just a matter of providing food--it is about investing in the well-being and future success of every child, regardless of their background or challenges. Maine's commitment to education should include ensuring that every student, in every setting, has the resources they need to succeed. Providing free school lunches to special purpose private schools is a necessary and positive step toward achieving this goal.
For these reasons, the MC-FFRF urges the committee to vote "OUGHT TO PASS" for LD 776. Thank you for your time and consideration.

TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF
L.D. 776
AN ACT TO PROVIDE FREE SCHOOL LUNCHES TO SPECIAL PURPOSE PRIVATE SCHOOLS THAT RECEIVE STUDENTS FROM THE PUBLIC SCHOOL SYSTEM
March 31, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Steven Bailey, the executive director of the Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association in support of L.D. 776.
Currently, Maine public school students and students attending a private school approved for tuition purposes and who participate in the National School Lunch program are provided lunch free of charge. These students attend these schools from the resident town, and receive this benefit for both breakfast and lunch.
As of now, this same benefit is not enjoyed by students who attend a special purpose private school. These students also are residents of the towns that make up their resident school administrative district, and attend these schools based on a placement decision by their Maine public school district.
Should the special purpose private school, receiving public funds for the students attending their school, also participate in the federal National School Lunch Program, it only seems right that these students should also be provided the same benefit as their peers in other Maine public schools and private schools approved for tuition purposes.
This appears to us to be a clean-up bill, making right what was previously not comparable for all Maine public school students across the state.
MSSA and MSBA both support the expansion of the meals at no cost to the student to the special purpose private schools, where they too must observe the criteria for eligibility within the statute.

Steven W. Bailey
MSBA Executive Director

Eileen E. King
MSSA Executive Director
